## Overview

This vignette illustrates an analysis of drug-related deaths in
Milwaukee County, Wisconsin, using `spHawkes`.

The packaged `milwaukee` dataset contains geocoded events classified as
drug-related deaths with recorded dates from 2020 onward. The accompanying
`milwaukee_county` object is the polygonal observation window. Both are
stored in NAD83 / UTM zone 16N (EPSG:26916), so spatial coordinates and
distance-based tuning parameters are expressed in metres.

The dataset is included as a reproducible worked example. It is not an
authoritative administrative release. See `?milwaukee` for data provenance,
construction details, and limitations.

The workflow covers exploratory plots, model fitting, diagnostics,
instantaneous intensity maps, a daily animation, and an annual
time-integrated intensity map. Code is displayed throughout so that the
analysis can be reproduced.

```{r packages}
library(spHawkes)
library(dplyr)
library(sf)
library(ggplot2)
```

## Data

```{r data}
milwaukee
milwaukee_county
```

There are `r nrow(milwaukee)` events in the dataset, spanning from
`r format(min(milwaukee$DeathDate), "%d %B %Y")` to
`r format(max(milwaukee$DeathDate), "%d %B %Y")`.

The event geometry is `POINT` and the observation window has
`r as.character(sf::st_geometry_type(milwaukee_county)[1])` geometry.
Both use EPSG:`r sf::st_crs(milwaukee)$epsg`.

## Exploratory patterns

### Monthly counts

The following series gives a first descriptive view of temporal
variation. The smooth is descriptive only; it is not part of the fitted
point-process model.

```{r monthly-counts, fig.height=4, fig.alt="Monthly counts of drug-related deaths with a descriptive smooth."}
monthly_counts <- milwaukee %>%
  st_drop_geometry() %>%
  count(death_month, name = "n_events")

ggplot(
  monthly_counts,
  aes(x = death_month, y = n_events)
) +
  geom_col(
    fill = "grey75",
    width = 25
  ) +
  geom_smooth(
    method = "loess",
    formula = y ~ x,
    se = FALSE,
    colour = "firebrick",
    linewidth = 0.9,
    span = 0.35
  ) +
  theme_minimal() +
  labs(
    title = "Monthly drug-related deaths in Milwaukee County",
    subtitle = "Events occurring from 2020 onward",
    x = NULL,
    y = "Number of deaths"
  )
```

### Event locations

```{r event-locations, fig.height=6, fig.alt="Locations of recorded drug-related deaths within the Milwaukee County boundary."}
ggplot() +
  geom_sf(
    data = milwaukee_county,
    fill = "grey95",
    colour = "grey35",
    linewidth = 0.5
  ) +
  geom_sf(
    data = milwaukee,
    colour = "firebrick",
    alpha = 0.30,
    size = 0.55
  ) +
  coord_sf(expand = FALSE) +
  theme_minimal() +
  labs(
    title = "Drug-related deaths in Milwaukee County",
    x = NULL,
    y = NULL
  )
```

The visible spatial heterogeneity motivates a model with a flexible
background intensity rather than a spatially homogeneous baseline.

## Fitting the model

`fit_semihawkes()` requires an `sf` object of point events, a polygonal
observation window, and the name of the date column. Since the data
are projected in metres, `cell_size`, `min_dist`, and `min_bandwidth`
below are also specified in metres.

The settings below prioritise a reasonably quick vignette build.
Only one EM iteration is used. The resulting fit illustrates the
workflow and should not be interpreted as a demonstrated converged
analysis.

For a substantive analysis, inspect convergence and assess stability
under more iterations and alternative tuning parameters. These include the
triggering kernel's spatial reach, which is left at its default of 1 km
here; it should be chosen with care for the process being studied (see
*Choosing the triggering reach* in `?fit_semihawkes`).

```{r fit, results="hide"}
cache_dir <- tempfile("spHawkes-milwaukee-")
dir.create(cache_dir)

fit <- fit_semihawkes(
  points = milwaukee,
  region = milwaukee_county,
  date_col = "DeathDate",
  cell_size = 500,
  cache_dir = cache_dir,
  bandwidth_args = list(
    k = 5,
    min_dist = 150,
    min_bandwidth = 300
  ),
  n_iter = 1,
  verbose = FALSE
)
```

```{r fit-summary}
summary(fit)

fit$n_iter
fit$stop_reason
```

Interpret the estimated background component jointly with the
self-exciting component. Spatial or temporal clustering alone does not
establish a triggering mechanism.

## Model components

The model separates the estimated intensity into time-varying and
spatial background components and a self-exciting contribution.
These plots provide a compact view of the fitted background components.

```{r components-weekly, fig.height=4, fig.alt="Estimated weekly background multiplier."}
plot(fit, which = "weekly")
```

```{r components-monthly, fig.height=4, fig.alt="Estimated monthly background multiplier."}
plot(fit, which = "monthly")
```

```{r components-trend, fig.height=4, fig.alt="Estimated long-term background trend."}
plot(fit, which = "trend")
```

```{r components-background, fig.height=6, fig.alt="Estimated spatial background surface in Milwaukee County."}
plot(fit, which = "background")
```

## Temporal goodness of fit

The temporal diagnostic compares observed event accumulation with
the accumulation implied by the fitted model. Here, `dt = 1` uses
a one-day discretisation.

```{r gof-time, fig.alt="Temporal goodness-of-fit diagnostic comparing observed and fitted event accumulation."}
gof_time <- gof_time_transform(
  fit,
  dt = 1
)

plot(gof_time)
```

Systematic discrepancies can indicate temporal structure not captured
by the fitted model. Agreement is evidence consistent with adequacy,
not proof that the proposed mechanism is correct.

## Spatial intensity snapshots

The fitted model can be evaluated on a spatial grid at selected times.
This is a separate step from fitting:
`background_trigger_grid()` uses the estimated components to calculate
background and triggering intensities at grid locations.

The workflow is:

1. Fit the model and retain `fit`.
2. Evaluate selected times and retain `grid_result`.
3. Plot or animate the evaluated snapshots.

The example below selects up to 15 consecutive days near the end of
the fitted observation window. Model times are measured in days since
`fit$events$start_date`.

We use 500 m spacing to keep the evaluation grid relatively small.
This grid is constructed separately from the background grid used
during fitting.

```{r intensity-grid}
model_origin <- as.Date(fit$events$start_date)

last_day <- floor(fit$events$TT)

selected_days <- seq.int(
  from = max(0, last_day - 14),
  to = last_day
)

grid_result <- background_trigger_grid(
  fit = fit,
  city = milwaukee_county,
  cell_size = 500,
  days = selected_days,
  nprocs = 1
)

snapshot_time <- selected_days[
  ceiling(length(selected_days) / 2)
]

snapshot_date <- model_origin + snapshot_time
```

### Total intensity

The total conditional intensity combines the background and triggering
components. This map is an instantaneous evaluation, not intensity
integrated over a full day.

```{r intensity-total, fig.height=6, fig.alt="Instantaneous total conditional intensity evaluated on a spatial grid."}
plot_intensity_snapshot(
  grid = grid_result,
  time = snapshot_time,
  component = "total"
) +
  labs(
    subtitle = paste(
      "Instantaneous evaluation on",
      format(snapshot_date, "%d %B %Y"),
      "- model day",
      snapshot_time
    )
  )
```

### Triggering intensity

The triggering map shows the fitted contribution of preceding events
at the selected time. It is a model-based conditional contribution,
not evidence that one death caused another.

```{r intensity-triggering, fig.height=6, fig.alt="Instantaneous triggering contribution evaluated on a spatial grid."}
plot_intensity_snapshot(
  grid = grid_result,
  time = snapshot_time,
  component = "triggering"
) +
  labs(
    subtitle = paste(
      "Instantaneous evaluation on",
      format(snapshot_date, "%d %B %Y"),
      "- model day",
      snapshot_time
    )
  )
```

These two static maps use separate colour scales. Their colours should
not be compared directly as if they represented the same numerical
values.

### Daily intensity animation

The same evaluated grid can be reused to generate an animation.
Each frame shows triggering intensity at one evaluated model time.
The colour scale is shared across frames.

The animation requires the optional `gifski` package, so the chunk below
is skipped when `gifski` is not installed rather than failing the build.
Install it to see the animation.

```{r milwaukee-intensity-gif, eval = requireNamespace("gifski", quietly = TRUE), cache=FALSE, out.width="100%", fig.cap="Daily snapshots of fitted triggering intensity in Milwaukee County.", fig.alt="Animated triggering intensity maps with a fixed colour scale across daily snapshots."}
dir.create(
  "figures",
  recursive = TRUE,
  showWarnings = FALSE
)

gif_file <- "figures/milwaukee-triggering-intensity.gif"

animate_intensity_snapshots(
  grid = grid_result,
  component = "triggering",
  filename = gif_file,
  fps = 3,
  width = 700,
  height = 600,
  overwrite = TRUE
)

stopifnot(
  file.exists(gif_file),
  file.info(gif_file)$size > 0
)

knitr::include_graphics(gif_file)
```

The chunk's code is shown either way. Where `gifski` is available the GIF
is regenerated and the animation appears above; where it is not, the code
is listed but not run.

Grid values are pointwise intensity evaluations, displayed as tiles
centred on the evaluation coordinates. The tiles are not clipped
to the county boundary.

## Annual time-integrated intensity

An instantaneous map describes intensity at one time. To summarise
a complete year while retaining the spatial dimension, integrate
the intensity over time:

\[
L_y(s)
=
\int_{a_y}^{b_y}
\widehat{\lambda}(s,t \mid \mathcal{H}_{t^-})\,dt,
\]

where \(a_y\) is 1 January of the selected year and \(b_y\) is
1 January of the following year.

This is an integral, not an annual average. Background and triggering
contributions are integrated separately.

### Select a complete year

The following code identifies calendar years fully covered by the
fitted observation window and selects the first one.

Both boundaries must lie inside the model window. We do not silently
replace a full year with a shorter interval.

```{r annual-period}
model_origin <- as.Date(fit$events$start_date)
model_end <- model_origin + floor(fit$events$TT)

candidate_years <- seq.int(
  from = as.integer(format(model_origin, "%Y")),
  to = as.integer(format(model_end, "%Y"))
)

candidate_starts <- as.Date(
  sprintf("%d-01-01", candidate_years)
)

candidate_ends <- as.Date(
  sprintf("%d-01-01", candidate_years + 1L)
)

candidate_start_times <- as.numeric(
  candidate_starts - model_origin
)

candidate_end_times <- as.numeric(
  candidate_ends - model_origin
)

complete_years <- candidate_years[
  candidate_start_times >= 0 &
    candidate_end_times <= fit$events$TT
]

if (!length(complete_years)) {
  stop("The fitted observation window contains no complete calendar year.")
}

annual_year <- complete_years[1L]

# To select another covered year, replace the line above, for example:
# annual_year <- 2021L

if (!(annual_year %in% complete_years)) {
  stop("The selected year is not fully covered by the fitted window.")
}

annual_start_date <- as.Date(
  sprintf("%d-01-01", annual_year)
)

annual_end_date <- as.Date(
  sprintf("%d-01-01", annual_year + 1L)
)

annual_start_time <- as.numeric(
  annual_start_date - model_origin
)

annual_end_time <- as.numeric(
  annual_end_date - model_origin
)

annual_year
annual_start_date
annual_end_date
```

The selected year is `r annual_year`. Its integration interval runs
from `r format(annual_start_date, "%d %B %Y")` to
`r format(annual_end_date, "%d %B %Y")`, with the latter date defining
the exclusive upper boundary.

### Evaluate and integrate

First evaluate instantaneous surfaces throughout the year.
Then pass the resulting grid to `integrate_intensity_period()`.

The daily time step below is an initial numerical approximation,
chosen to keep the worked example manageable, as is the coarser 1 km
spatial grid: evaluating a whole year of daily surfaces is the most
expensive step in this vignette. The endpoint is included because the
trapezoidal rule uses evaluations at both boundaries.

```{r annual-intensity-integration}
integration_step <- 1

annual_times <- sort(unique(c(
  seq(
    from = annual_start_time,
    to = annual_end_time,
    by = integration_step
  ),
  annual_end_time
)))

annual_grid <- background_trigger_grid(
  fit = fit,
  city = milwaukee_county,
  cell_size = 1000,
  days = annual_times,
  nprocs = 1
)

annual_intensity <- integrate_intensity_period(
  grid = annual_grid,
  start = annual_start_time,
  end = annual_end_time
)

annual_intensity$period
annual_intensity$integration$method
```

Integration uses actual time differences between evaluations.
It therefore accommodates the different durations of ordinary and
leap years without dividing by the number of days.

### Annual total intensity map

The integrated object contains one surface per component.
Its single snapshot is identified by the initial model time.

We reuse the plotting function and explicitly change the labels
to distinguish the integral from an instantaneous intensity.

```{r annual-total-map, fig.height=6, fig.alt="Total fitted intensity integrated over the selected calendar year, retaining its spatial distribution."}
plot_intensity_snapshot(
  grid = annual_intensity,
  time = annual_start_time,
  component = "total"
) +
  labs(
    title = paste(
      "Time-integrated total intensity:",
      annual_year
    ),
    subtitle = paste(
      format(annual_start_date),
      "to",
      format(annual_end_date),
      "(exclusive)"
    ),
    fill = "Integrated intensity"
  )
```

### Annual triggering contribution

The same integrated object can be used to inspect the annual
triggering contribution without reevaluating the model.

```{r annual-triggering-map, fig.height=6, fig.alt="Fitted triggering intensity integrated over the selected calendar year."}
plot_intensity_snapshot(
  grid = annual_intensity,
  time = annual_start_time,
  component = "triggering"
) +
  labs(
    title = paste(
      "Time-integrated triggering intensity:",
      annual_year
    ),
    subtitle = paste(
      format(annual_start_date),
      "to",
      format(annual_end_date),
      "(exclusive)"
    ),
    fill = "Integrated intensity"
  )
```

Use `component = "background"` to display the integrated background
contribution. The static maps have separately determined colour scales.

### Interpretation and numerical accuracy

These maps retain spatial variation after integrating over time.
They are not event counts per cell: obtaining a cell-level contribution
to the compensator would additionally require spatial integration.

The calculation uses the observed history throughout the selected
year. It is a retrospective integrated conditional intensity, not
a forecast made at the beginning of that year.

The trapezoidal rule integrates the sampled surfaces. It is not an
exact event-aware integration procedure, and triggering intensity can
change discontinuously at event times. For substantive use, assess
stability with a finer temporal evaluation grid rather than assuming
that daily evaluations are sufficient.

Evaluations also inherit the temporal and spatial triggering cutoffs
of `background_trigger_grid()`. Those settings should be reviewed
alongside the time step and spatial resolution.

## Reproducibility and limitations

The construction code for the packaged datasets is available in
`data-raw/make-milwaukee-data.R` in the package source. It filters the
underlying release to drug-related deaths dated from 2020 onward with
valid geocodes that intersect the Milwaukee County boundary.

Nothing in this vignette is cached: the model fit, the evaluated grids,
the annual integral and the GIF are all recomputed each time the vignette
is built, so they reflect the installed version of the package.

This example demonstrates the workflow of `spHawkes`; it should not
be treated as a definitive epidemiological or policy analysis. In
particular, geocoding uncertainty, administrative classification,
changes in reporting, and unobserved covariates can generate spatial
and temporal patterns that resemble self-excitation.

Only one EM iteration is used here. All fitted surfaces, diagnostics,
and integrated maps should therefore be interpreted as illustrative
outputs rather than results from a demonstrated converged fit.
